title: Northern Illinois University CITL, Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction
text:
## Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction

Robert Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction are a sequence of instructional events that align with and support the internal cognitive processes of learning. A top instructional designer uses them as a checklist for structuring any lesson.

## 1. Gain Attention of the Students

Ensure the learners are ready to learn and participate in activities by presenting a stimulus to capture their attention. Methods include stimulating novelty, uncertainty, and surprise, posing thought-provoking questions, having students pose questions to peers, and running ice breaker activities.

## 2. Inform Students of the Objectives

Inform students of the objectives or outcomes for the course and individual lessons to help them understand what they are expected to learn and do. Recommended approaches: describe the required performance, establish performance criteria collaboratively, and include course objectives on assessment prompts.

## 3. Stimulate Recall of Prior Learning

Help students make sense of new information by relating it to something they already know or something they have already experienced. Techniques include questioning about previous experiences, discussing prior concept understanding, connecting past course content to current topics, and incorporating earlier learning into present activities.

## 4. Present the Content

Use strategies to present and cue lesson content to provide more effective instruction. Strategies include presenting content through multiple formats (video, demonstration, lecture, podcast, group work), employing varied media, incorporating active learning, and providing access for external review.

## 5. Provide Learning Guidance

Help students learn how to learn. Methods include offering scaffolded instructional support, modeling diverse learning strategies (mnemonics, concept mapping, role playing, visualization), using examples and non-examples, and providing case studies, visual images, analogies, and metaphors.

## 6. Elicit Performance (Practice)

Have students apply what they have learned to reinforce new skills and knowledge and to confirm correct understanding of course concepts. Methods: facilitate activities with deep-learning questions, peer collaboration, laboratory exercises, formative assessments (assignments, projects, presentations), and quizzes and tests that emphasize comprehension over mere recall.

## 7. Provide Feedback

Provide timely feedback of students' performance to assess and facilitate learning and to allow students to identify gaps in understanding before it is too late. Feedback types include confirmatory (encouragement without improvement guidance), evaluative (accuracy information without guidance), remedial (directing toward correct answers), and descriptive or analytic (providing improvement suggestions), plus peer and self-evaluation approaches.

## 8. Assess Performance

Test whether the expected learning outcomes have been achieved on previously stated course objectives. Methods: pre- and post-tests, embedded formative opportunities (questioning, activities, quizzes), varied assessment methods for multiple demonstration opportunities, and objective rubrics.

## 9. Enhance Retention and Transfer

Help learners retain more information by providing them opportunities to connect course concepts to potential real-world applications. Techniques include avoiding content isolation through conceptual connections, incorporating previous test questions in subsequent exams, converting learned information across formats (for example creating concept maps that demonstrate idea relationships), and aligning learning activities with clearly articulated lesson goals.

title: University of Illinois Chicago CATE, Bloom's Taxonomy of Educational Objectives
text:
## Bloom's Taxonomy: Educational Objectives Framework

Bloom's Taxonomy originated in 1956 when Benjamin Bloom chaired a meeting of university educators who created a hierarchical model used for classifying learning objectives by levels of complexity and specificity. The original framework identified three learning domains: cognitive (thinking), affective (emotional growth), and psychomotor (physical skills). The initial cognitive version used noun-based terminology for six hierarchical levels progressing from foundational to advanced thinking.

## 2001 Anderson & Krathwohl Revision

The most significant update converted the framework from nouns to verbs, to reflect active learning. The revised six-level cognitive domain became:

1. Remember: retrieve relevant knowledge from memory
2. Understand: determine the meaning of instructional messages
3. Apply: use a procedure in a given situation
4. Analyze: break materials into components and determine how they work together
5. Evaluate: make judgments based on criteria and standards
6. Create: create a new or original work

The revision also swapped the top two levels: Evaluation moved to level five and Synthesis (renamed Create) moved to the top.

## Two-Dimensional Structure (the Knowledge Dimension)

Anderson and Krathwohl added a knowledge dimension with four components: Factual Knowledge (basic disciplinary elements), Conceptual Knowledge (interrelationships within larger contexts), Procedural Knowledge (disciplinary methods), and Metacognitive Knowledge (self-aware learning processes). This matrix lets designers combine a cognitive process with a knowledge type for comprehensive learning design.

## Action Verbs for Learning Objectives

Each level aligns to action verbs for measurable objectives:

Remember: define, identify, list, name, recall, recognize, reproduce
Understand: classify, describe, explain, interpret, paraphrase, summarize, translate
Apply: calculate, demonstrate, modify, operate, perform, practice, solve
Analyze: categorize, compare, contrast, diagram, distinguish, examine, separate
Evaluate: appraise, argue, assess, critique, defend, evaluate, justify
Create: assemble, compose, construct, design, devise, formulate, generate

## Affective and Psychomotor Domains

The affective domain has five levels progressing from passive reception through value internalization: Receiving, Responding, Valuing, Organizing, Characterizing. The psychomotor domain (Simpson's version) has seven levels ranging from sensory perception through origination of novel procedures.

## Implementation Strategy

Instructors craft learning objectives by selecting a domain, determining the complexity level, and choosing aligned action verbs, creating observable, measurable student outcomes. A common anti-pattern is writing objectives with unmeasurable verbs like understand or know, which cannot be observed or assessed.

title: Florida State University College of Medicine, Behavioral Objectives and How to Write Them (Mager's model)
text:
## Mager's Model for Writing Behavioral Objectives

Robert Mager's influential 1962 model defines the standard for writing performance objectives that a top instructional designer applies before designing any instruction. As Mager states, an objective is a description of a performance you want learners to be able to exhibit before you consider them competent.

## Three Core Components

An effective objective requires three parts:

1. Measurable action verb (Performance): the performance must be observable and quantifiable, describing what the learner can actually DO.
2. Specified Conditions: the circumstances under which the performance occurs, such as tools, references, constraints, or environmental factors (if relevant).
3. Criterion for Success: the standard of acceptable competency, for example accuracy, speed, or quality level.

Mager's fuller framing is often taught as the ABCD model: Audience (who the learner is), Behavior (an overt, observable behavior, even if the actual behavior is covert or mental), Condition (the circumstances of performance), and Degree (the criterion, the acceptable level of performance).

## Observable and Measurable Requirement

Objectives must describe observable, measurable performance. Fuzzy verbs like understand, know, appreciate, or grasp are not observable and cannot be assessed; they must be replaced with overt action verbs such as construct, demonstrate, calibrate, retrieve, identify, prepare, and examine.

## Concrete Examples

General and weak: The learner will be able to prepare appropriate new patient workups.

Specific and strong: The learner will prepare legible, comprehensive, focused workups including a chronologically organized present illness, comprehensive physical exam with pertinent detail, a unified problem list, differential diagnosis, and treatment plan.

Another example: The student will correctly name the five stages of mitosis (the criterion of correctly is implicit).

## Note on Components

Conditions and criteria are often implicit rather than explicitly stated, depending on the instructional purpose, but the performance verb must always be observable. Writing objectives this way is the anchor of alignment: assessment and content are later checked against the objective.

title: Jacksonville State University Online, Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning
text:
## Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning

Richard E. Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning is the evidence base every e-learning designer works from. It rests on three core assumptions about how the mind processes multimedia.

## Three Core Assumptions

1. Dual Channels: there are two separate channels, auditory and visual, for processing information (related to dual-coding theory).
2. Limited Capacity: each channel has a finite capacity, similar to Sweller's cognitive load.
3. Active Processing: learning is an active process of filtering, selecting, organizing, and integrating information based upon prior knowledge.

## The Twelve Multimedia Principles

1. Coherence Principle: people learn better when extraneous words, pictures, and sounds are excluded rather than included.
2. Signaling Principle: people learn better when cues that highlight the organization of the essential material are added.
3. Redundancy Principle: people learn better from graphics and narration than from graphics, narration, and on-screen text.
4. Spatial Contiguity Principle: people learn better when corresponding words and pictures are placed near rather than far from each other on the page or screen.
5. Temporal Contiguity Principle: people learn better when corresponding words and pictures are presented simultaneously rather than successively.
6. Segmenting Principle: people learn better when a multimedia lesson is presented in user-paced segments rather than as a continuous unit.
7. Pre-training Principle: people learn better from a multimedia lesson when they know the names and characteristics of the main concepts beforehand.
8. Modality Principle: people learn better from graphics and narration than from animation and on-screen text.
9. Multimedia Principle: people learn better from words and pictures than from words alone.
10. Personalization Principle: people learn better when words are in conversational rather than formal style.
11. Voice Principle: people learn better when the narration is a friendly human voice rather than a machine voice.
12. Image Principle: people do not necessarily learn better when the speaker's image is added to the screen.

## How a Master Applies This

Mayer groups these principles by the type of processing they manage: reducing extraneous processing (coherence, signaling, redundancy, spatial contiguity, temporal contiguity), managing essential processing (segmenting, pre-training, modality), and fostering generative processing (multimedia, personalization, voice, image). Loading both channels (narrated visuals) beats overloading one channel (text plus the same words read aloud), which is why the redundancy principle warns against reading on-screen text verbatim.

title: University of Florida IFAS, What is Understanding by Design (Wiggins & McTighe)
text:
## Understanding by Design (UbD) and Backward Design

Understanding by Design, by Grant Wiggins and Jay McTighe, is built on backward design: you start from the desired results, then the evidence, then the activities, the reverse of the common habit of starting from activities or the textbook. UbD names that common habit the twin sins of design: activity-oriented design (fun tasks with no clear learning goal) and coverage-oriented design (marching through content to cover it all, with no priorities). A master instructional designer avoids both.

## Stage 1: Identify Desired Results

Examine content standards and develop instructional objectives, prioritizing content for logical flow. Key questions: what should learners be able to do, know, and understand at the end of instruction, and what long-term, enduring understandings are desired. Enduring understandings are the big ideas that have lasting value beyond the classroom; essential questions are open, provocative questions that point at those big ideas and drive inquiry.

## Stage 2: Determine Acceptable Evidence

Plan how to collect evidence of learning BEFORE selecting teaching methods, thinking like an assessor. Create assessments aligned with the desired results. Central questions: how will I know if learners have achieved the desired results, and what is acceptable evidence of achievement.

## Stage 3: Plan Learning Experiences and Instruction

Only after outcomes and assessments are set do you design purposeful activities that lead to the Stage 2 evidence, considering learners' prior knowledge for scaffolding.

## Six Facets of Understanding

Genuine understanding is revealed through six facets: Explanation (describing how things work and why events occurred), Interpretation (making meaning through narratives, data, and experiences), Application (using knowledge in new real-world situations), Perspective (seeing through multiple critical viewpoints), Empathy (understanding others' feelings and worldviews), and Self-Knowledge (knowing the limits of one's own understanding).

## WHERETO Elements

WHERETO guides Stage 3 planning: Where the learners are headed and Why; Hook and hold attention; Equip learners with the experiences, tools, and knowledge to meet the goals; Rethink and Revise; allow learners to Evaluate their work; Tailor to individual needs, interests, and styles; Organize the sequence for deep understanding and engagement.

title: Kirkpatrick Partners, The Kirkpatrick Model (Four Levels of Evaluation)
text:
## The Kirkpatrick Model of Training Evaluation

The Kirkpatrick Model, created by Don Kirkpatrick and updated as the New World Kirkpatrick Model, is the most widely used framework for evaluating training. A top instructional designer designs evaluation into a program from the start, not as an afterthought.

## Level 1: Reaction

The degree to which the target audience finds an experience or initiative favorable, engaging, relevant, and supportive. Relevance is emphasized as a key predictor of behavior transfer. Do not wait until the end of the program to survey; use formative pulse checks. The New World model adds engagement, relevance, and customer satisfaction as Level 1 measures.

## Level 2: Learning

The degree to which the target audience acquires the intended knowledge, skills, attitude, confidence, and commitment based on their participation. Beyond traditional pre and post tests, measurement includes confidence and commitment as early predictors of on-the-job performance.

## Level 3: Behavior

The degree to which the target audience applies what they learned during training when they are back on the job, that is, whether they perform the critical behaviors in their environment. Measurement must occur soon after learning to enable course correction. Behavior change depends on required drivers: processes and systems that reinforce, monitor, encourage, and reward performance of critical behaviors, such as manager check-ins, job aids, and rewards.

## Level 4: Results

The degree to which targeted organizational outcomes occur as a result of the experience or initiative. Because Level 4 results can take time, the model uses leading indicators: short-term observations and measurements that suggest critical behaviors are on track to create the desired results.

## Strategic Approach: Plan Backward

Organizations should plan from Level 4 to Level 1, that is, start with the desired outcomes and work backward to design for them, so evaluation drives design rather than following implementation. The Performance Environment acts as both a foundation and an influencer and can support or block progress across all levels. This aligns with backward design: a common anti-pattern is measuring only Level 1 smile sheets and declaring training a success while nothing changes on the job (Levels 3 and 4).

title: Chartered College of Teaching (Impact), Cognitive Load Theory and its Application (Sweller)
text:
## Cognitive Load Theory

Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), introduced by John Sweller, formalizes the instructional implications of the limits of working memory. Working memory has a small, limited capacity; long-term memory, where schemas are stored, is effectively unlimited. The core prescription: total cognitive load must remain within working-memory capacity, or learning quality degrades. As Reif puts it, the cognitive load involved in a task is the cognitive effort required by a person to perform it.

## Three Types of Cognitive Load

Intrinsic load: the inherent difficulty of the material itself, driven by element interactivity (how many elements must be held in mind at once) and by the learner's prior knowledge.

Extraneous load: load generated by the way material is presented, when the presentation does not support learning. This is the load a designer can and should reduce through better design.

Germane load: the effort devoted to processing information and building schemas in long-term memory, the productive load.

## Named Effects a Master Knows Cold

Worked Example Effect: showing complete, step-by-step solutions before learners attempt new problems reduces cognitive strain during initial learning, because a worked example reduces the number of interacting elements a novice must consider.

Split-Attention Effect: when different sources of information about the same topic are separated in time or space (for example a diagram with a key placed away from the text it explains), learners must mentally integrate them, which generates extraneous load. The fix is integrating text into the diagram.

Expertise Reversal Effect: instructional supports (like worked examples) that help novices can reduce effectiveness for experts, who find the extra information redundant. Guidance that helps beginners can hurt experts.

## Caveats and Limitations

Over-reducing load is also a risk: excessive simplification can break learning into too many trivial small steps. And cognitive load is difficult to measure directly, as Doug Holton notes, which makes the theory hard to prove empirically even though its design prescriptions (reduce extraneous load, use worked examples, avoid split attention) are well supported.

title: InstructionalDesign.org, The ADDIE Model
text:
## The ADDIE Model

ADDIE stands for Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation. Originally developed at Florida State University in the 1970s, it is the foundational process model most other instructional design models refine. A master uses it as a systematic backbone, not a rigid script.

## Analysis

Clarify the instructional problem, establish goals and objectives, and identify the learning environment and the learners' existing knowledge and capabilities. Key questions address the audience, desired behavioral outcomes, constraints, delivery options, and timelines. This is where you decide whether training is even the right solution.

## Design

Focus on learning objectives, assessment instruments, exercises, content, and subject-matter analysis. This phase should be systematic and specific: document the design strategy, choose instructional approaches aligned to the behavioral domains (cognitive, affective, psychomotor), and produce storyboards, interface design, prototypes, and the visual design.

## Development

Create and assemble the content assets described in the Design phase, integrate technologies, then debug and revise based on feedback and pilot review.

## Implementation

Prepare facilitators and learners: train facilitators on the curriculum, outcomes, delivery methods, and tools, and ready the learners. Ensure all materials, sites, and systems are functional.

## Evaluation

Evaluation has two parts. Formative evaluation is present throughout each phase (reviews, pilot tests, feedback). Summative evaluation happens after implementation, using criterion-referenced assessment and opportunities for user feedback, to measure whether the solution met its goals.

## Limitations

The classic weakness of ADDIE is that treating the phases as a strictly linear waterfall makes it slow and inflexible: problems surface late, after expensive development. This critique gave rise to rapid prototyping and to iterative alternatives like SAM (Successive Approximation Model), which front-load prototyping and feedback.

title: University of Iowa Tippie College, Merrill's First Principles of Instruction
text:
## Merrill's First Principles of Instruction

M. David Merrill's First Principles of Instruction (2002) distill what recurs across the major instructional design theories. Merrill argued that learning is promoted when instruction is problem-centered and when learners move through four phases of learning: activation, demonstration, application, and integration. Learning is promoted in proportion to how fully instruction implements these principles.

## The Problem-Centered (Task-Centered) Core

Instruction should center on authentic, real-world problems or whole tasks that learners are likely to encounter, not on isolated topics or fragmented objectives. Learners should engage in progressively more complex whole tasks, not just component skills studied in isolation.

## The Five Principles

1. Problem-Centered / Task-Centered: learning is promoted when learners work on real-world, whole problems and see the task they will be able to do.
2. Activation: learning is promoted when learners activate relevant prior knowledge and experience as a foundation for the new knowledge, through recall, relating, or describing previous experience.
3. Demonstration (Show me): learning is promoted when the instruction demonstrates or shows what is to be learned (worked examples, expert performances, modeling, case studies) rather than merely telling information about it, and the demonstration is consistent with the objective.
4. Application (Let me): learning is promoted when learners apply their new knowledge to solve problems, with coaching and corrective feedback that is gradually withdrawn, and the practice is consistent with the objective (recall for facts, do the procedure for procedures).
5. Integration: learning is promoted when learners integrate the new knowledge into their world, through reflection, discussion, defending, or by getting to publicly demonstrate the new skill.

These principles operate cyclically and iteratively across increasingly demanding tasks. Merrill's implicit anti-pattern is tell-and-test instruction: information presented then quizzed, with no demonstration, no authentic application, and no integration.

title: Learning-Theories.com, Keller's ARCS Model of Motivational Design
text:
## Keller's ARCS Model of Motivational Design

John Keller's ARCS model treats motivation as a design problem, not luck. Motivation must be built into instruction across four components: Attention, Relevance, Confidence, and Satisfaction. A top designer diagnoses which of the four is missing when learners disengage.

## 1. Attention

Capture and sustain interest. Perceptual arousal uses surprise, novelty, incongruity, and uncertain events to gain interest. Inquiry arousal stimulates curiosity by posing challenging questions or problems to be solved. Variability sustains attention by varying the presentation format. Practical methods: active participation through games and role play, mixing videos, lectures, and discussion, modest humor, presenting conflicting viewpoints, concrete examples, and problem-posing.

## 2. Relevance

Connect the content to the learner's own goals and experience. Six strategies: Experience (connect new material to existing competencies), Present Worth (show immediate applicability, what it does for me today), Future Usefulness (show long-term value), Needs Matching (address achievement, risk-taking, power, and affiliation motives), Modeling (demonstrate desired behavior through examples and mentors, guest speakers, peer tutoring), and Choice (offer multiple pathways to complete work).

## 3. Confidence

Build the learner's belief that success is possible and within their control. Provide clear performance objectives and evaluation standards, meaningful achievement opportunities, incremental progression from easy to hard, and constructive feedback. Learners should feel some degree of personal control over their learning and assessment, so they attribute success to their own effort and ability.

## 4. Satisfaction

Make learning feel rewarding so motivation is sustained. Let learners use their new skills in a real or simulated setting (intrinsic reinforcement), provide reinforcement and feedback and appropriate extrinsic rewards, keep rewards equitable and consistent, and avoid excessive praise for trivial effort, which undermines credibility. Keller pairs the model with a systematic design process: define, design, develop, evaluate.

title: Chartered College of Teaching (Impact), The Problem with Learning Styles (debunking the meshing hypothesis)
text:
## Anti-Pattern: The Learning Styles Myth

One of the most important things a genuine top instructional designer knows cold is that learning styles are a debunked neuromyth. Designing separate materials for visual, auditory, or kinesthetic learners wastes effort and is not supported by evidence.

## The Meshing Hypothesis

The meshing hypothesis (also called the matching hypothesis) is the idea that catering to a learner's favored sensory preference, their learning style, will improve learning: for example that self-identified visual learners will learn better with visual instruction and auditory learners better by listening. It has intuitive appeal but has been exposed as a neuromyth.

## The Evidence (Pashler et al.)

Harold Pashler, Mark McDaniel, Doug Rohrer, and Robert Bjork established the methodological standard: to justify learning styles, researchers would need a crossover design showing that different instructional methods optimize the test scores of different types of learners. That is, self-identified visual learners must outperform auditory learners when taught visually, and vice versa. Reviewing the literature, they found no adequate evidence base to justify incorporating learning-styles assessments into general educational practice, and the few properly designed studies contradicted the hypothesis. Rogowsky et al., testing it with the proper crossover methodology, found participants had no significant advantage when taught using their preferred learning style. The existence of a preference says nothing about what that preference implies for how someone should be taught.

## Why It Persists and Why It Matters

About 90 percent of surveyed English language teachers in the US and Canada still believe the meshing hypothesis despite the debunking. Continued endorsement of learning styles interferes with the development of evidence-based practice, diverting resources into VAK assessments over three decades and away from empirically supported strategies such as the ten identified by Dunlosky et al. (like retrieval practice and spaced practice). The evidence-based move is to match the modality to the content, not to the learner: a map is best shown visually to everyone, a poem is best heard by everyone.

title: Allen Interactions, Rapid Instructional Design and Development with SAM (Michael Allen)
text:
## SAM: The Successive Approximation Model

SAM, created by Dr. Michael Allen, is the agile, iterative alternative to ADDIE, emphasizing rapid prototyping and collaborative development. It addresses ADDIE's weakness (a long, linear analysis-heavy waterfall where problems surface too late) by cycling through evaluate, design, develop continuously.

## Three Phases

Preparation Phase: gather essential background information quickly, prioritizing accessibility over exhaustiveness, deliberately avoiding lengthy upfront analysis. It launches with the Savvy Start, a brainstorming session that assembles decision-makers, budget holders, subject-matter experts, supervisors, and prospective learners to validate assumptions and generate initial design concepts.

Iterative Design Phase: expand the Savvy Start ideas through successive design cycles under a breadth-before-depth principle, so teams do not over-develop one area prematurely. Prototypes progress from media prototype (visual style) to functional prototype (interactivity) to integrated prototype. Tasks are prioritized as Threshold (mandatory), Target (expected), Future (deferred), and Epic (post-launch).

Iterative Development Phase: produce increasingly refined versions: Design Proof (functional demonstration on the intended platform), Alpha (complete implementation of all content and media), Beta (alpha corrected from validation feedback), and Gold (final release).

## Contrasts with ADDIE

SAM minimizes upfront analysis, expecting productive analysis to emerge during the cycles. Instead of exploring unlimited alternatives, the team asks Why shouldn't we do this? to focus on specific issues. Design backward from the advanced skills you want, prioritizing learner engagement over content organization. The trade-off: SAM makes many small iterative steps, whereas ADDIE makes fewer large steps based on heavy analysis.

title: The Learning Scientists, Retrieval Practice (the Testing Effect)
text:
## Retrieval Practice (the Testing Effect)

Retrieval practice is one of the most robust findings in the science of learning and a core tool for any top instructional designer building assessments and practice. It means recreating something you learned in the past from memory and thinking about it right now, ideally after a delay so you have partly forgotten it. Passive re-reading is insufficient.

## Why It Beats Re-reading

Practicing retrieval makes information more retrievable later. Compared with simply looking over notes, if you practice retrieval you are more likely to remember the information later and more likely to be able to use and apply it in new situations. The act of pulling information OUT of your head strengthens memory more than putting information IN through re-reading or re-listening. This is why quizzing, not just presenting, must be designed into instruction.

## Six Ways to Build Retrieval In

1. Practice tests and questions answered without consulting the materials.
2. Self-generated questions created from the content.
3. Flashcards, with genuine retrieval and no peeking.
4. Free recall: writing down everything you can remember about a topic.
5. Memory sketching: drawing concepts from memory.
6. Concept mapping from memory, linking ideas with explanatory relationships.

## The Key Caveat

Retrieval practice can be HARD, and that difficulty is the point (a desirable difficulty): the effort of recall is what produces durable, transferable learning. An anti-pattern is treating a course as delivery only (present content, then a token recall check); a master schedules repeated low-stakes retrieval across the experience.

title: The Learning Scientists, Spaced Practice (Distributed Practice)
text:
## Spaced Practice (Distributed Practice)

Spaced practice means spreading study and review over time rather than cramming it into one block (massed practice). As the Learning Scientists put it, five hours spread out over two weeks is better than the same five hours right before the exam. Designing spacing into a curriculum, revisiting earlier material across sessions, is a hallmark of expert learning design.

## Why Cramming (Massed Practice) Fails

Three problems with cramming: it is time-inefficient, requiring more total study time for equivalent learning; information learned by cramming is quickly forgotten after the exam, which matters because future learning depends on previous learning; and cramming replaces sleep, which is very important for learning and for mental and physical health.

## How to Implement Spacing

Start early with short, regular sessions. Review material one day after each class rather than immediately, so a little forgetting occurs. Continue studying before exams, but distribute sessions across weeks. Use effective strategies like retrieval practice rather than re-reading. Deliberately return to important older information to maintain retention.

## Forgetting as a Tool

Counterintuitively, you need to forget a little bit in order to benefit from spaced practice. The small effort of re-retrieving partly-forgotten material is what strengthens the memory, which connects spacing directly to retrieval practice: they are strongest used together. Cramming feels productive because material is fluent in the moment, which is exactly the illusion of competence a designer must design against.

title: W3C Web Accessibility Initiative, Accessibility Principles (WCAG / POUR)
text:
## Accessible Learning: The WCAG POUR Principles

Every learning experience must be accessible. The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) organize accessibility under four principles, POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. A top instructional designer bakes these in from the start rather than retrofitting.

## Perceivable

Information and user interface components must be presentable to users in ways they can perceive. Provide text alternatives (equivalents) for non-text content: short alt text for images, icons, buttons, and graphics, and descriptions for charts and diagrams. Provide text transcripts and captions for audio, and audio descriptions (narrations of important visual details) for video. Mark up headings, lists, tables, and input fields properly so content adapts. Do not use color as the only way of conveying information, and ensure default foreground and background color combinations provide sufficient contrast.

## Operable

User interface components and navigation must be operable. All functionality available by mouse must also be available by keyboard. Let users stop, extend, or adjust time limits and pause, stop, or hide moving, blinking, or scrolling content. Do not include content that flashes at rates and patterns known to cause seizures. Give pages clear titles and descriptive section headings, and more than one way to find relevant pages. Support touch, voice/speech input, and gestures.

## Understandable

Information and the operation of the interface must be understandable. Identify the primary language of a page and provide definitions for unusual words, phrases, idioms, and abbreviations. Keep navigation that repeats across pages in the same place each time (predictable). Offer descriptive instructions, error messages, and suggestions for correction.

## Robust

Content must be robust enough to be interpreted reliably by a wide variety of user agents, including assistive technologies. Ensure markup can be reliably interpreted and provide a name, role, and value for non-standard interface components.

## Conformance Levels

WCAG defines three conformance levels: A (minimum), AA (the common legal and organizational target), and AAA (highest). Most learning content aims for WCAG 2.1 or 2.2 Level AA. The anti-pattern is treating accessibility as a compliance checkbox at the end: captions bolted on, alt text auto-generated and meaningless. Accessible design (clear structure, captions, contrast, keyboard access) helps all learners, not only those with disabilities.

title: Training Industry, The 70-20-10 Model for Learning and Development
text:
## The 70-20-10 Model

The 70-20-10 model describes how people, especially managers, actually build capability: about 70 percent of knowledge from job-related experiences, 20 percent from interactions with others, and 10 percent from formal educational events. It reminds instructional designers that a formal course is only a small slice of how learning really happens.

## Origins

Morgan McCall, Michael M. Lombardo, and Robert A. Eichinger developed the framework in the 1980s at the Center for Creative Leadership in Greensboro, North Carolina, from research into the key developmental experiences of successful managers.

## The Three Components

70 percent, experiential (on-the-job): employees discover and refine job-related skills, make decisions, address challenges, and interact with influential people such as managers and mentors. This is where most durable learning happens.

20 percent, social: coaching, mentoring, collaboration, and peer interaction, providing consistent encouragement and feedback.

10 percent, formal: structured courses and workshops, which add value but contribute less than experiential and social methods.

## How a Master Uses It (and Its Critiques)

The model is a general guideline, not a precise prescription: designers use it to justify supporting on-the-job practice, job aids, coaching, and social learning rather than pouring everything into a course. Contemporary critiques note the ratios lack a rigorous universal empirical basis and shift with technology and how people work; researchers propose an OSF (on-the-job, social, formal) ratio that varies by industry, organization, and learner. The practical lesson stands: if 90 percent of capability forms outside formal training, design for the workflow (performance support, practice, reinforcement), not just the event.

title: xAPI.com, Action Mapping (Cathy Moore)
text:
## Cathy Moore's Action Mapping

Action Mapping, developed by Cathy Moore in 2008, is the discipline that keeps instructional design honest: it forces every design decision back to a measurable business result and to what people need to DO, not what they need to know. It is the antidote to the information dump.

## The Four Steps

1. Identify the business goal: establish a measurable organizational objective as the foundation for the whole design. A lot of e-learning and other training interventions happen without a real business goal in mind, and that is the root problem Action Mapping fixes.
2. Identify what people need to DO: determine the specific, observable actions people must take on the job to reach that goal.
3. Design practice activities: create exercises that let learners rehearse each necessary behavior, mirroring the real world as closely as possible.
4. Identify the minimum information: establish only what people need to know to complete each activity. If a piece of information does not support an activity, omit it.

## Core Philosophy and the Anti-Pattern It Kills

Action Mapping rejects the traditional knowledge-centric approach to training, prioritizing behaviors over information transfer, which produces far more practical and realistic activities. Crucially, it challenges whether training is needed at all: Cathy Moore's flowchart (Do they really need training?) routes many problems to non-training fixes like a job aid, a process change, or better tools, because if the cause is not a genuine skill gap, a course will not help. Paired with xAPI, Action Mapping lets you measure whether the intervention actually changed the target behavior and business outcome, not just whether people clicked through slides.

title: Devlin Peck, Scenario-Based Learning: The Complete Guide
text:
## Scenario-Based Learning

Scenario-based learning (SBL) puts learners inside a realistic situation where they make decisions and experience the consequences, rather than memorize information. It is grounded in situated learning theory: learning sticks best when it happens in the same authentic context where it will be applied. Instead of telling learners about judgment, SBL lets them practice it safely with immediate feedback.

## The Three Cs of Every Scenario

Challenge: a realistic workplace situation that requires a decision.
Choice: multiple plausible options, not one obvious answer surrounded by obvious wrong distractors.
Consequence: real outcomes that result from the decision, shown to the learner rather than narrated by a mentor character telling them they were wrong.

## The Complexity Spectrum

Mini scenarios (a single decision with immediate feedback), branching scenarios (multiple decision points with diverging and converging paths), gamified or immersive scenarios (branching plus scoring, characters, and stakes), and AI role-play simulations (open conversations). Depth of consequence beats length of path.

## When to Use SBL, and When Not To (the Anti-Pattern)

Use scenarios when mistakes carry real cost (safety, financial, legal), when judgment matters more than memorization, when high-stakes conversations need practice, or when motivation is low and content feels dry. Skip scenarios when the gap is purely informational (build a job aid instead), when environmental factors cause poor performance (fix the systems, not training), or when a checklist would suffice. This is the same discipline as Action Mapping: do not build a scenario, or any course, for a problem that is not a skill gap.

## Design Process

Action map first (identify observable, high-priority job behaviors before outlining content). Transform each priority action into a decision with plausible choices and visible consequences. Storyboard in editable text before building slides. Prototype visuals separately. Test one representative scene before scaling. Avoid exponential branching: three choices across four fully branched decisions creates 81 endings; instead let choices produce different consequences then reconverge learners at the next shared challenge.

## Measuring Success

Track decisions, not completions. Record which choices learners select, where they struggle first, and whether on-the-job behavior changes. Completion is a vanity metric; the choices learners make reveal where real-world confusion lives.

title: InstructionalDesign.org, Andragogy (Malcolm Knowles, Adult Learning)
text:
## Andragogy: Knowles's Adult Learning Theory

Malcolm Knowles's andragogy is the theory of how adults learn, distinct from pedagogy (teaching children). It matters because most workplace instructional design is for adults, who bring different needs and motivations. Its core: adults are self-directed and expect to take responsibility for their own decisions.

## Core Assumptions About Adult Learners

1. Adults need to know why they need to learn something before they invest in it.
2. Adults need to learn experientially: their accumulated experience, including their mistakes, is a rich resource for learning.
3. Adults approach learning as problem-solving, not as absorbing a body of content.
4. Adults learn best when the topic is of immediate value and relevance to their job or life.

Knowles also frames adult learners as moving from dependence toward self-direction and as internally rather than externally motivated.

## Design Principles That Follow

Adults should participate in the planning and evaluation of their own instruction. Experience, including mistakes, provides the basis for learning activities. Instruction should be problem-centered rather than content-oriented, and focused on subjects with immediate relevance. Favor case studies, role-playing, simulations, and self-evaluation, with the instructor acting as a facilitator and resource rather than a lecturer. The anti-pattern is treating adult professionals like empty vessels in a lecture, ignoring their experience and their need to know why the training matters to their work.

title: Simply Psychology, Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory and Cycle
text:
## Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory

David Kolb defines learning as the process whereby knowledge is created through the transformation of experience (1984). Knowledge emerges through actively engaging with experience, not by passively receiving information. This underpins hands-on, reflective learning designs.

## The Four-Stage Learning Cycle

1. Concrete Experience: the learner engages in a hands-on activity or encounters a new situation, the foundation for learning.
2. Reflective Observation: the learner reviews what happened and considers how it aligns with or conflicts with existing understanding.
3. Abstract Conceptualization: through reflection, the learner forms or refines mental models, theories, and general principles.
4. Active Experimentation: the learner tests the new concepts in real or simulated situations to validate understanding.

Effective learning requires progressing through all four stages; no single stage suffices on its own. A well-designed learning experience gives learners something to do, time to reflect, a model or concept to make sense of it, and a chance to apply it.

## The Four Learning Styles

Kolb combines two dimensions, perception (feeling vs thinking) and processing (watching vs doing), into four styles: Diverging (feel and watch: imaginative, people-oriented, good at brainstorming), Assimilating (think and watch: logical, idea-focused, good at organizing information and theory), Converging (think and do: practical problem-solving, applying concepts to technical tasks), and Accommodating (feel and do: action-oriented, hands-on, adapts readily). Note: unlike the debunked VAK learning styles, Kolb's styles describe preferences within a cycle every learner should complete, not a prescription to teach each person in only one mode.

title: Queen Mary University Academy, Constructive Alignment (John Biggs)
text:
## Constructive Alignment (Biggs)

Constructive alignment, coined by John Biggs in 1999, is an approach to curriculum design that closely aligns teaching and assessment to the intended learning outcomes. It is the academic sibling of backward design and the single most important quality check on any learning design: do the objectives, the activities, and the assessment all line up?

## The Core Principle

The learning activity named in the intended outcome, expressed as a verb, must be activated in the teaching if the outcome is to be achieved, and it must be present in the assessment task to verify that the outcome has in fact been achieved. If the outcome says learners will analyze, then the teaching must have them analyzing and the assessment must ask them to analyze, not to merely recall.

## The Three Aligned Components

1. Intended Learning Outcomes (ILOs), formulated first: clear statements, expressed as action verbs, of what students should be able to do.
2. Teaching and Learning Activities: designed so students actively engage in the very activity the outcome names.
3. Assessment Tasks: structured to verify that the intended outcomes were actually achieved.

## Constructivist Foundation and Backwash

The framework rests on constructivism: students construct knowledge for themselves through what they do, so what the student does is just as important as what the teacher does. Biggs uses the term backwash: students naturally learn what they anticipate will be assessed, so misaligned assessment quietly teaches the wrong thing. The classic anti-pattern constructive alignment prevents is an objective that promises high-level skill (apply, evaluate) paired with an assessment that only tests recall, a misalignment that makes the whole course dishonest about what it develops.

title: Don Clark (knowledgejump.com), van Merrienboer's 4C/ID Model
text:
## The 4C/ID Model (Four-Component Instructional Design)

Jeroen van Merrienboer's 4C/ID model (with Paul Kirschner) is the go-to blueprint for teaching genuinely complex skills, the kind where component skills must be integrated and coordinated, not learned in isolation. It is a corrective to atomized, topic-by-topic design that never adds up to real-world competence.

## The Four Components

1. Learning Tasks: concrete, authentic, whole-task experiences that form the backbone of the curriculum and promote schema construction through mindful abstraction from concrete experience. Tasks are organized into task classes and sequenced by increasing difficulty, with clear performance objectives.
2. Supportive Information: the information that supports the non-recurrent (variable, reasoning-based) aspects of a task. It bridges prior knowledge and new tasks, establishing non-arbitrary relationships between new elements and what learners already know, including cognitive strategies and mental models. It is the theory, the how-to-approach-this-problem knowledge.
3. Procedural / Just-in-Time (JIT) Information: prerequisite procedural knowledge for the recurrent (routine, rule-based) aspects, delivered exactly when needed and then faded. It embeds procedural information in step-by-step rules.
4. Part-Task Practice: additional repetitive practice for selected recurrent aspects that must reach high automaticity (for example, drilling a routine until it is automatic), so working memory is freed for the whole task.

## Key Design Principles

Whole-task learning with scaffolding: learners work on whole meaningful tasks from the start, and support fades as competence increases. Task complexity progresses across task classes of increasing complexity with decreasing scaffolding. The model deliberately distinguishes supportive information (for non-recurrent, novel reasoning) from JIT procedural information (for recurrent, routine steps), because those two kinds of skill are learned differently. The anti-pattern 4C/ID fights is teaching many isolated sub-skills and facts and hoping learners assemble them into competent performance on their own, which rarely happens; whole-task practice with fading support builds transfer.

title: Microlearning Beyond Boundaries: A Systematic Review (Heliyon / PMC)
text:
## Microlearning: Definition and Evidence Base

This systematic review defines microlearning as an instructional approach that delivers targeted, action-oriented, bite-sized content to achieve specific objectives within a short period, typically within a few seconds or minutes. Its defining characteristics: a single learning objective per module (action-oriented, learner-centered), bite-sized self-contained units, a short timeframe (studies report roughly 1 to 15 minutes), and need-based, just-in-time delivery. Related terms include bite-sized learning, snippet learning, and just-in-time learning, with microlearning the predominant term (appearing 2,247 times across the analyzed studies).

## Theoretical Foundation

Microlearning is grounded in Sweller's Cognitive Load Theory: cognitive load is the amount of information working memory can hold at once, and breaking content into bite-sized units helps manage intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load. When total cognitive load is manageable, educators can guide learners' attention toward the processes that matter for learning. It pairs naturally with spaced practice.

## Evidence-Based Benefits

Cognitive outcomes: knowledge acquisition, retention, recall, and transfer, plus improved critical thinking and better test performance versus traditional methods. Behavioral outcomes: higher completion rates and engagement, better task performance, skill development. Affective outcomes: increased motivation, satisfaction, self-efficacy, and reduced anxiety. One finding: knowledge was comparable between online distance microlearning and traditional face-to-face active learning.

## Limitations and Anti-Patterns

The review is explicit about failure modes a top designer must respect. Cognitive Overload Risk: McNeill and Fitch highlight overload when there are too many objectives, excessive content, or lengthy activities, in other words, microlearning done wrong reintroduces the very overload it should prevent. Fragmented Learning: learners can experience fragmented experiences and struggle without prior background knowledge. Complex Content: some critics question microlearning's ability to deliver complex, integrated topics, which is where whole-task models like 4C/ID fit better. Engagement Dependency: effectiveness hinges on actual use; relevance decline causes participation to drop in later modules. Subject Variation: effectiveness differs significantly by subject. The core anti-pattern: chopping a long course into short pieces is not microlearning; each unit must stand alone around one objective, or you just get a library of disconnected clips nobody uses.
